title: HelioSearch follow-up: usage spike + 429s (Dedicated options)
summary: Follow-up call after HelioSearch hit sustained token growth and multiple 429 rate-limit errors on Redwood Hosted. HelioSearch described a production search + answer experience with higher concurrency during weekday peaks and longer contexts than expected. Redwood (AE+SE) reviewed current usage patterns, why 429s occur (rate limits + burst behavior), immediate mitigations (quota/rate adjustments, client retries, backoff, streaming, batching guidance), and a Dedicated path for predictable throughput and isolation. Agreed on a benchmark plan and a pricing/packaging follow-up, plus a shorter technical deep dive on autoscaling/SLAs.
topics: What changed: usage spike, new customer rollout, concurrency patterns
429s: where they occur, retry behavior, user impact
Workload details: model choice, context lengths, token/output mix, peak QPS
Mitigations on Hosted: rate limits, ramping, caching/batching suggestions
Dedicated overview: predictable throughput, autoscaling, SLAs, isolation
next_steps: Redwood to provide a benchmark template + recommended test matrix (short/long context, peak concurrency) and a simple load-gen script suggestion.
HelioSearch to share last-7d traffic pattern (hourly concurrency), typical prompt/context sizes, and target p95 latency by endpoint.
Redwood to send Dedicated overview + ballpark pricing ranges and recommended starting capacity (with assumptions stated).
Redwood to apply a temporary Hosted quota bump for 7 days (guardrailed) while the benchmark runs, and confirm updated 429 thresholds.
Schedule a 30-min Dedicated technical deep dive focused on autoscaling policy + failure/fallback behavior.
action_items: Stephanie Nguyen - Send Dedicated overview deck + pricing guardrails (ballpark) - due 2025-05-07
Markus Klein - Send benchmark plan + success criteria and recommended load test approach - due 2025-05-08
Ryan Chen (HelioSearch) - Share traffic/concurrency chart and representative payloads (prompt + max tokens) - due 2025-05-09
Maya Patel (HelioSearch) - Confirm internal timeline + procurement constraints and who joins next call - due 2025-05-09
Stephanie Nguyen - Coordinate temporary Hosted limit bump and confirm in email - due 2025-05-06
transcript:
Fireflies.ai - Transcript

Title: HelioSearch follow-up: usage spike + 429s (Dedicated options)
Date/Time: 2025-05-06 10:03 AM PT
Duration: 38 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees:
- Stephanie Nguyen (Redwood Inference, AE)
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference, Solutions Engineer)
- Maya Patel (HelioSearch, Head of Engineering)
- Ryan Chen (HelioSearch, ML Engineer)
- Olivia Stone (HelioSearch, Product)

---

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Hey Maya, hey Ryan, Olivia. Can you all hear us okay?

[00:03] Maya Patel: Yep, we’re good.

[00:04] Ryan Chen: Yeah.

[00:06] Markus Klein: Loud and clear.

[00:08] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool. Thanks for jumping on. This is a follow-up from the 429s and the usage spike we saw last week. I pulled some notes from our side, but mostly we want to understand what changed and then talk through options. Markus is here to go deeper on the technical side.

[00:23] Olivia Stone: Great. Yeah, the timing is good because we had a bit of a fire drill.

[00:27] Stephanie Nguyen: Yeah, we saw the alerts. Before we dive in, quick agenda: what changed in your workload, where the 429s show up, what’s the business impact, and then we’ll cover immediate mitigations on Hosted and then the Dedicated path if you want predictable capacity. Sound okay?

[00:43] Maya Patel: Works.

[00:44] Ryan Chen: Yep.

[00:45] Markus Klein: Perfect.

[00:47] Stephanie Nguyen: Alright. Maya, do you want to start with what changed? The last time we talked you were in a smaller beta.

[00:55] Maya Patel: Yeah. So we rolled out to… I guess “GA” for two customers on Monday, and then we added another integration partner that same week. Basically our traffic went from kind of spiky but small to like sustained. And then weekday mornings are just… high.

[01:14] Olivia Stone: The product is search with an answer, so there’s a query, we retrieve, then we call the model to synthesize. And we added more context into the prompt because the first version was missing some citations.

[01:27] Markus Klein: Got it, so more retrieved docs in the prompt.

[01:30] Ryan Chen: Exactly. We increased the number of chunks. Also we turned on streaming, which helps UX, but it didn’t fix the 429 issue.

[01:39] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s helpful. On the 429s, are you seeing them as outright failures or are you retrying and they recover?

[01:46] Ryan Chen: Mixed. We do retries but honestly our backoff is probably not great. It’s like… we retry fast, and then the user sees either a delay or sometimes it errors.

[01:58] Maya Patel: It’s not acceptable for us because it’s in the critical path. We can’t have 2% of requests failing on a Monday morning.

[02:06] Markus Klein: Yeah. And the 429s you see, are they from Redwood directly? Like HTTP 429? Or are you also getting timeouts upstream?

[02:14] Ryan Chen: Mostly 429 from you, and then a couple timeouts on our side because we hold the request open.

[02:20] Olivia Stone: The painful part is it happens right when people are demoing.

[02:24] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood. Let’s talk quickly about what 429 means on Hosted for Redwood. It’s basically “we’re protecting you and the system” against bursts beyond the account’s current limits. We can adjust limits, but the core thing is your workload is getting into a regime where bursts and sustained concurrency matter.

[02:41] Markus Klein: And it’s not just tokens per day. It’s concurrency and request shape. Like, if your context length doubled, your per-request compute footprint changes a lot.

[02:52] Ryan Chen: Yeah that tracks.

[02:54] Markus Klein: Can I ask a few questions to size it? Roughly how many requests per second at peak and what’s your typical prompt length and output length.

[03:04] Ryan Chen: Peak, maybe 15 to 25 RPS during the morning? But it’s bursty. Like a single tenant might do a bunch at once.

[03:13] Maya Patel: We’re multi-tenant but not super evenly distributed.

[03:16] Ryan Chen: Prompt length… hmm. It depends. If we include like 8 chunks it can be like 6k to 10k tokens input? And output is smaller, like 300 to 700 tokens.

[03:28] Markus Klein: Okay, 6k-10k prompt, that’s non-trivial. And model, you’re on… is it the Redwood hosted “RWI-Chat-7B” profile or the bigger one? Sorry I might be misnaming it.

[03:39] Ryan Chen: We’re on Llama… 70B. I think your catalog lists it as “Llama 3 70B Instruct” or something.

[03:46] Markus Klein: Yep, that’s the one.

[03:48] Stephanie Nguyen: And you’re currently in the self-serve plan on Hosted, correct?

[03:52] Maya Patel: Yes. We started self-serve and it was fine, but now it’s hurting.

[03:56] Olivia Stone: We also looked at OpenAI as a fallback, but we’d rather not change providers if we can avoid it.

[04:02] Stephanie Nguyen: Makes sense. We can talk about the tradeoffs there too.

[04:05] Markus Klein: Another question: are you doing one call per user request? Or multiple calls? Like rerank + generate + something else.

[04:12] Ryan Chen: For this path it’s one generate call. We do embeddings separately but that’s not spiking the same way.

[04:18] Markus Klein: Got it. And do you have any caching at the prompt prefix level? Like system prompt + instructions that’s consistent across calls.

[04:25] Ryan Chen: Not really. We have a template, but we don’t have caching across requests. It’s mostly unique because of retrieval.

[04:32] Markus Klein: Totally. There still might be some reuse in the instruction prefix, but retrieval dominates.

[04:38] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. So immediate options: 1) we can raise the Hosted limits and help you set better backoff so 429s don’t turn into user-facing failures, and 2) if this is the new normal, Dedicated gives you predictable throughput and isolation.

[04:54] Maya Patel: Can we do option 1 quickly? Like today?

[04:57] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes. We can do a temporary bump while we evaluate. We just want to do it responsibly so we don’t create new failure modes. Markus, can you speak to the retry patterns?

[05:07] Markus Klein: Yeah. For 429, you want exponential backoff with jitter, respect Retry-After if present. And you also want to cap the max concurrency on the client side, otherwise you get the “thundering herd” where retries just amplify.

[05:22] Ryan Chen: We definitely have the thundering herd. We do like three retries within a second.

[05:27] Markus Klein: Yeah, that’s going to hammer. If you can, do something like 200ms, 500ms, 1s, 2s with jitter. And more importantly, use a queue so you smooth the burst.

[05:40] Maya Patel: We can do that. But the bigger issue is we actually need the throughput. Like, it’s not just a spiky thing. It’s sustained every weekday.

[05:49] Stephanie Nguyen: Right. That’s where Dedicated becomes relevant.

[05:52] Olivia Stone: What does Dedicated change, in practical terms? Like will it just… not 429?

[05:58] Markus Klein: You can still overload anything, but the behavior changes because you have reserved GPU capacity sized to your workload. We set an autoscaling policy (within guardrails), and the throttling is now mostly your own configured limits, not multi-tenant constraints.

[06:14] Stephanie Nguyen: And you get predictable throughput and SLA options. Hosted is great for getting started, but when you’re in production with real peaks, Dedicated is where you get the “no surprises” capacity story.

[06:26] Maya Patel: Okay. What’s the typical setup? Like number of GPUs?

[06:30] Markus Klein: It depends on target p95 and your context lengths. With 70B and 10k input tokens, you’re compute-heavy on prefill. So we’d want to benchmark. But as a starting point, some customers start with a small pool—say 2 to 8 GPUs depending on hardware—then set autoscaling for peaks.

[06:47] Ryan Chen: Is this H100 or A100?

[06:49] Markus Klein: We can do both, and also L40S for some workloads, but for 70B with long context you’ll likely want H100 class for the best latency/cost. We’ll propose options.

[07:02] Ryan Chen: We care about p95. Right now we’re like 3-4 seconds sometimes, and our goal is under 2 seconds for most requests. But that’s with streaming, so… you know.

[07:11] Markus Klein: Understood. When people say “2 seconds,” we should clarify: time-to-first-token vs time-to-complete. Streaming makes UX feel fast if TTFT is low.

[07:21] Olivia Stone: Yeah, exactly. We want the first token quick, and we don’t want the whole thing to take like 20 seconds.

[07:27] Markus Klein: For long prompts, TTFT can be the pain because prefill takes time.

[07:33] Stephanie Nguyen: Can I ask about the business side for a sec? Are these paid end users today, or still a free tier?

[07:39] Maya Patel: Paid. Two customers are paid, the partner integration is… rev share, but it’s still real usage.

[07:46] Stephanie Nguyen: Got it. And timeline—are you expecting another rollout this month?

[07:50] Olivia Stone: Yes, we have three more customers in pipeline. If the product doesn’t fall over.

[07:56] Maya Patel: So we need a plan this week.

[08:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. Then I think we should run a quick benchmark to size Dedicated and also to validate we can hit your TTFT goals. Markus can outline a benchmark plan.

[08:10] Markus Klein: Yep. The benchmark we recommend: pick 3 request shapes—small context (2k), medium (6k), large (10k)—and 2 output sizes (300 and 800 tokens). Then run at concurrency levels like 5, 10, 20, maybe 30, depending on your peak. Measure TTFT and tokens/sec.

[08:29] Ryan Chen: We can do that. How do we run it? We have our own load tool but it’s not great.

[08:35] Markus Klein: We can share a simple k6 or Locust script. Also we can do a joint run from our side if you share sanitized prompts, like structure with fake content. We don’t need your customer data.

[08:48] Maya Patel: Prefer sanitized. We have some restrictions.

[08:51] Stephanie Nguyen: Totally fine. We also have a privacy-aware approach here. We don’t need PII or proprietary docs. Just lengths and patterns.

[08:59] Ryan Chen: Okay.

[09:01] Markus Klein: One more: are you using function calling or structured outputs?

[09:05] Ryan Chen: Not function calling. We do JSON-ish output but it’s not strict.

[09:09] Markus Klein: Okay. If you later need strict JSON, that can also affect retries and sometimes token counts.

[09:17] Olivia Stone: We might, but not yet.

[09:19] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s talk about Dedicated pitch at a high level, and then we’ll get you pricing ranges. Dedicated means: reserved GPU pool, you get isolation, predictable throughput, optional burst capacity, and we can do a region guarantee if needed. For your case, the main driver is reliability and scaling, right?

[09:38] Maya Patel: Yes. And honestly, we also want fewer surprises on cost. We had a day where spend jumped and it wasn’t clear to us what happened.

[09:46] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep, that’s a common trigger. Dedicated tends to be a commit model, so you have more predictability. We’ll still give token-level breakdowns, but the budget is less volatile.

[09:58] Ryan Chen: We also saw you have “prefix cache” or KV cache? I read something in docs.

[10:04] Markus Klein: Yeah, KV cache is per-request for generation. We also have some caching options, but in your workload with retrieval it’s not huge unless your instruction prefix is heavy and repeated. Batching, on the other hand, can help if you can accept a little queuing.

[10:21] Ryan Chen: We can accept small queueing, but the product is interactive.

[10:25] Markus Klein: Right, so we keep the batch window small. It’s a classic trade: throughput vs latency.

[10:32] Stephanie Nguyen: On the 429s specifically, I want to make sure you know this wasn’t “your account is broken.” It’s that you exceeded the current limits. We’ll fix it, but we need to align plan to reality.

[10:44] Maya Patel: Understood. It’s just… painful.

[10:47] Olivia Stone: Can you explain why it started happening only now? Like we didn’t change the code that much.

[10:53] Markus Klein: Two things likely: concurrency increased, and prompt length increased. Both increase compute usage. The model’s “prefill” time scales with input length. So even if RPS is only 20, if every request is 10k tokens input, that’s heavy.

[11:10] Ryan Chen: Yeah we probably doubled input length.

[11:12] Markus Klein: That’ll do it.

[11:14] Stephanie Nguyen: Also, we saw a few bursts that looked like 3-4x your baseline for short windows. That’s where backoff matters.

[11:21] Ryan Chen: That’s likely one tenant doing a bulk operation.

[11:25] Maya Patel: We should put a cap per tenant too.

[11:27] Markus Klein: That’s a good idea.

[11:30] Stephanie Nguyen: Can we talk about your architecture quickly? Do you have a job queue or is it synchronous end-to-end?

[11:36] Ryan Chen: Synchronous. User searches, we do retrieval, then LLM call, then respond.

[11:41] Markus Klein: Okay. Then you’re sensitive to tail latency. Dedicated helps because it reduces contention and makes throughput predictable.

[11:49] Olivia Stone: If we do Dedicated, is it a big engineering change?

[11:53] Markus Klein: Usually minimal. Same API surface, but you get a different endpoint/route and config. You can pin model versions more tightly, and there are some knobs for autoscaling and fallbacks. But client integration should be straightforward.

[12:08] Ryan Chen: Okay.

[12:10] Stephanie Nguyen: Another question: any data residency or compliance constraints? I know you’re search for… which vertical again? Sorry.

[12:17] Maya Patel: We’re in B2B knowledge search. Some customers are in finance-adjacent. Nothing like HIPAA, but they ask about SOC2 and retention.

[12:26] Stephanie Nguyen: We can provide SOC2, and Dedicated can give you more isolation. If you ever need VPC/Private, that’s another path, but I don’t think you’re asking for that today.

[12:37] Maya Patel: Not right now. Just… stable.

[12:40] Markus Klein: Cool.

[12:41] (crosstalk)

[12:42] Olivia Stone: Also pricing. Like, I know you can’t give exact numbers on a call, but we need ranges.

[12:48] Stephanie Nguyen: Totally. I can give ballparks with assumptions, and then after we benchmark we’ll finalize. Generally Dedicated is a monthly commit based on the capacity tier. For your use case, I suspect it’s not tiny, but we’ll right-size.

[13:05] Maya Patel: Is there a minimum term?

[13:07] Stephanie Nguyen: Typically monthly or annual depending on tier. For pilots we can do shorter evaluation terms. We’ll work with you.

[13:15] Ryan Chen: What about just increasing Hosted limits permanently? Like why not do that.

[13:21] Markus Klein: We can, but Hosted is still shared capacity. You’ll still see more variance and you’ll still be subject to platform-level guardrails. Dedicated makes the performance envelope more controllable.

[13:33] Stephanie Nguyen: And from a commercial standpoint, once you’re spending at this level, Dedicated often reduces unit cost if configured well.

[13:41] Ryan Chen: Okay. We also tested OpenAI for a bit and it was stable but expensive. And Anthropic too. But we like the open model path.

[13:52] Markus Klein: Yeah, many teams do that. One note: if you keep the option to fall back to OpenAI for emergencies, we can talk about multi-provider fallback patterns. But within Redwood, we can also do fallback to a smaller compatible model variant if that’s acceptable for some endpoints.

[14:10] Olivia Stone: We’d rather degrade quality than error, for some percent of traffic. Like if we can show a shorter answer instead of failing.

[14:18] Markus Klein: That’s actually a great strategy. We can set a fallback policy: if queue depth exceeds X, route to a smaller model or shorten max tokens. But that’s a product decision.

[14:31] Maya Patel: That would be okay for non-enterprise tenants.

[14:34] Stephanie Nguyen: We can include that in a plan.

[14:37] Markus Klein: For the benchmark, we can also test the smaller model for “degraded mode.”

[14:42] Ryan Chen: Makes sense.

[14:44] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s focus on getting you stable now. I’m going to propose: we bump Hosted limits today for 7 days, you improve retries/backoff, and we run the benchmark over the next 48-72 hours to size Dedicated.

[15:00] Maya Patel: That sounds good.

[15:02] Olivia Stone: What do you need from us to do the bump?

[15:05] Stephanie Nguyen: Just confirmation of the peak behavior and that you’ll implement backoff. Also, if you can tell us your expected peak RPS, so we don’t set it too low.

[15:14] Ryan Chen: Peak maybe 25 RPS today, but could be 40 if a tenant does bulk.

[15:20] Markus Klein: For bulk, consider moving it async. But yes.

[15:24] Maya Patel: Noted.

[15:26] Markus Klein: Another thing: do you have per-route separation? Like search-answer vs internal admin tasks.

[15:32] Ryan Chen: Not separate endpoints, but we can tag them.

[15:36] Markus Klein: If you can separate, we can apply different rate limits and fallback policy. That helps.

[15:43] Ryan Chen: Okay.

[15:45] (audio glitch)

[15:47] Stephanie Nguyen: Sorry, I think someone cut out for a second.

[15:49] Olivia Stone: I’m here.

[15:51] Ryan Chen: Same.

[15:52] Markus Klein: All good.

[15:55] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool. Markus, can you go a bit deeper on what Dedicated implementation looks like? Like how fast can we stand it up.

[16:03] Markus Klein: Typically, once commercial is aligned, we can provision in days, not weeks. You get a Dedicated endpoint, and we work with you on model pinning and autoscaling. For the pilot, we can do a small pool and measure your real traffic, then adjust.

[16:20] Maya Patel: Okay. We might need security review but it’s not huge.

[16:25] Stephanie Nguyen: We can send SOC2 and the standard docs. But again, sounds like you’re not asking for Private or VPC now.

[16:33] Maya Patel: Correct.

[16:35] Olivia Stone: When you say autoscaling, is it like a Kubernetes thing? Or…

[16:39] Markus Klein: Under the hood yes, but what you see is policy knobs: min/max capacity, scale-up thresholds based on queue depth or utilization, and we can set “burst” behavior. It’s not you managing K8s.

[16:55] Ryan Chen: Okay.

[16:56] Markus Klein: Also we’ll talk about the “SLO” you care about—TTFT, p95, error rate—and we tune the batching window and concurrency limits to hit it.

[17:07] Ryan Chen: Great.

[17:09] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s check on success criteria. Maya, what do you need to see to feel good about moving to Dedicated?

[17:16] Maya Patel: No 429s in normal operation, obviously. And p95 first token under 1.5 seconds, ideally. And then cost that is not… like, it can’t double from current.

[17:28] Olivia Stone: Also a clear story for our customers. Like “we upgraded capacity” so it’s stable.

[17:34] Markus Klein: Great. We can measure TTFT in the benchmark and also estimate cost based on throughput. On cost, Dedicated can actually improve if you have sustained load because you avoid some inefficiencies of bursty shared capacity.

[17:48] Ryan Chen: We also have a question about max context. We might go to 16k.

[17:54] Markus Klein: We can support larger contexts depending on model and configuration, but performance will change. We should include a 16k case in the benchmark if that’s really coming.

[18:06] Ryan Chen: It’s likely. Our retrieval team wants more chunks.

[18:10] Markus Klein: Okay.

[18:11] Stephanie Nguyen: One more question: do you have a hard deadline? Like a customer commitment date.

[18:18] Maya Patel: Next Monday we have an exec demo to a big prospect, and we cannot have errors.

[18:24] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood. Then we’ll focus on immediate stability. Dedicated might not be fully provisioned by Monday depending on procurement, but we can get Hosted stable for that demo and have Dedicated ready quickly after.

[18:39] Olivia Stone: That works.

[18:40] Markus Klein: Also for Monday, we can set conservative max tokens and enforce per-tenant caps to reduce risk.

[18:47] Ryan Chen: We can do that.

[18:50] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. I’ll send a recap email after this with the plan and the tasks. While we’re here, quick question: do you have someone on your side who will run the benchmark? Ryan, is that you?

[19:01] Ryan Chen: Yeah, I can run it.

[19:03] Markus Klein: Cool. I’ll send a template and a script suggestion.

[19:06] Ryan Chen: Thanks.

[19:08] Olivia Stone: Can we talk about pricing a bit more? Like if it’s crazy we need to know.

[19:13] Stephanie Nguyen: Totally. Without being too hand-wavy: if your peak is 25-40 RPS with 6k-10k prompts on 70B, you’re in a “serious” tier. But we’ll propose two options: one optimized for TTFT (more capacity) and one optimized for cost (slightly more queueing). And you can pick.

[19:33] Maya Patel: That’s what we need.

[19:35] Stephanie Nguyen: Also we’ll talk about whether a smaller model can handle some traffic. If yes, that reduces the required capacity.

[19:44] Ryan Chen: We tested 8B and quality wasn’t there.

[19:47] Markus Klein: Maybe 13B or a different instruction model could be acceptable for fallback only. Not primary.

[19:53] Olivia Stone: Yeah fallback is okay.

[19:56] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.

[19:58] Markus Klein: One last technical question: Are you seeing 429s across all regions or are you pinned?

[20:03] Ryan Chen: We’re pinned to us-west.

[20:05] Markus Klein: Okay. Dedicated can also be pinned, or multi-region if you want. But let’s keep it simple.

[20:13] Maya Patel: Simple is good.

[20:15] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. I think we have a plan. Before we wrap, anything else on your side?

[20:21] Olivia Stone: Just want to confirm we’re not going to get spammed by sales emails. No offense.

[20:25] Stephanie Nguyen: None taken. You’ll get one recap email from me and then a pricing email. We’ll coordinate. If you prefer a single thread, we’ll keep it tight.

[20:35] Maya Patel: Appreciate it.

[20:37] Ryan Chen: Yeah.

[20:38] Markus Klein: And if you hit 429s again after we bump, ping us immediately. There’s a limit to how high we can go on Hosted, but we can tune.

[20:47] Stephanie Nguyen: Exactly. Also if you want, we can join your Slack Connect, but that’s optional.

[20:52] Maya Patel: Let’s do email first.

[20:54] Stephanie Nguyen: Sounds good.

[20:56] Markus Klein: I’ll send the benchmark doc today. It’ll include the metrics we care about: TTFT, p50/p95, throughput, and error rate.

[21:04] Ryan Chen: Great.

[21:05] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect. We’ll do a quick follow-up call end of week to review benchmark results and decide on Dedicated. How’s Thursday morning?

[21:13] Maya Patel: Thursday 10 works.

[21:15] Olivia Stone: Works.

[21:16] Ryan Chen: Yep.

[21:17] Stephanie Nguyen: Great, I’ll send the invite.

[21:20] Markus Klein: Thanks all.

[21:21] Maya Patel: Thanks.

[21:22] Olivia Stone: Thanks.

[21:23] Ryan Chen: Bye.

---
